positioning_statement: For the rescue dog owner who has already spent a drawer's worth of money on calming products that didn't work — who dreads October, wrestles a whippet into a coat built for a Labrador, and quietly suspects she is somehow failing her dog — this is anxiety kit built on a different promise. Every product is road-tested on a panel of twelve genuinely anxious rescues before it goes on sale, with the fail rate published; the feeder took three redesigns, and they say so. Instead of a Prime delivery that arrives tomorrow and slides off in forty seconds, you get kit sized for your actual dog's build, a handwritten guide on how to introduce it slowly, and someone who answers your DMs themselves. Premium because this is your last attempt, not your first — and because your dog isn't broken, he has just never had something built for dogs like him.
message_pillars: The person buying this kit isn't really shopping for a coat — she's trying to get her evenings in October back, to book a weekend away without dreading it, and to stop quietly believing she has somehow failed the dog she chose.

Every product is tested on twelve genuinely anxious rescue dogs and the fail rate is published — so when the coat reaches your door, it has already been through the versions that didn't work, and you don't have to be.
When it works, she folds the coat up the next morning with something between relief and disbelief — and then opens her phone to tell her rescue group, unprompted, that this one is actually different.
differentiators: Rescue-tested with published failures, not just a pass mark (E3): "Every product goes through a trial panel of twelve genuinely anxious rescue dogs before launch, and we publish the fail rate — the feeder took three redesigns and we say so."
Fit, guidance, and a real person at the other end (E3): "Sizing videos for odd-shaped rescues, a handwritten intro guide in every box, and I answer the DMs myself."
value_props: Instead of a £14 Amazon wrap that slides off a whippet chest in forty seconds, you get a coat sized against odd builds and tested on genuinely anxious dogs before it was ever sold.

Instead of another product that promised calm and lives in the drawer, you get kit with a published trial record — including the redesigns that failed — so you know exactly what survived to reach you.

Instead of figuring out alone how to introduce something new to a nervous dog, you get a handwritten guide in the box that already knows your dog needs slow, and a founder who answers the DMs when it matters.

tone_rules: Keep most sentences under 20 words. A longer sentence earns its length by carrying a specific, concrete detail — not a general claim. Write as you would explain something to a worried person at a kitchen table, not as you would fill a product listing.

No clinical or marketing jargon. 'Anxiety management solution' becomes 'something that actually helps him settle.' 'Calming protocol' becomes 'how to introduce it.' Test every word: would a worried dog owner find it reassuring, or distancing? Use the plain, kind register of a vet behaviourist's handout.

Own the premium price without apology or inflation. Say what it buys in concrete terms — twelve rescue dogs tested it, the failures are published, the coat fits his actual build. Never hedge with 'yes it's more expensive but', and never run a discount without a reason that genuinely serves the buyer.

Warmth is not levity. You can be wry about the industry's failures — the drawer, the diffuser that made the hallway smell odd and did nothing — never about a dog's fear or the person who has been carrying it. A frightened dog is not a hook.
Sounds like a vet behaviourist who also owns a rescue and remembers exactly which drawer you mean, not a sponsored post written by someone who has never met a frightened dog.
banned_words: take your business to the next level

elevator_pitch: Anxious rescue dogs get kit road-tested on twelve real nervous rescues — and the failures are published. Every coat is sized for odd builds, every box ships with a handwritten guide on introducing things slowly, and the founder answers the DMs. So instead of another drawer of things that didn't work, you get your evenings in October back.
